newsitem.title: UK: HORSE RACING-WORLD CUP WINNER SINGSPIEL LAYS SECONDITIS GHOST.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-WORLD CUP WINNER SINGSPIEL LAYS SECONDITIS GHOST.

text.p: Dubai World Cup winner Singspiel has laid the ghost of "seconditis "and now stands proud as the biggest European money winner in history.
Thursday's victory in the world's richest race added another $2.4 million to the coffers to raise the total haul to around $5.4 million.
"He' s a star," enthused his Newmarket trainer Michael Stoute after Singspiel, ridden by Jerry Bailey, outfought the American pair of Siphon and Sandpit.

But Stoute also recalled times last season and before that when Singspiel seemed fated be the bridesmaid not the bride. In one period the horse was involved in six photo finishes, losing five of them.

One of his most notable losses came last October in the Breeders' Cup Turf to stable companion Pilsudski. But that was swiftly forgotten a month later when Singspiel carried Frankie Dettori to victory in the Japan Cup.
Singspiel is now in the super league and deservedly so. His record in his last 12 races now reads six wins and six seconds, a model of consistency if ever there was one.

After last Saturday's wash-out Singspiel's owner, Sheikh Mohammed, the man who created the World Cup concept, was rewarded with victory in his own race. Of the many thousands of racehorses to pass through his hands in the last 15 years or so, Singspiel must now hold a special affection.

Trainer Stoute has started this year where he left off -- on top of the international pile. Not many trainers are likely to emulate his Woodbine International-Breeders' Cup-Japan Cup-World Cup four-timer.
Jockey Bailey thought nothing would ever equal winning last year's inaugural race on Cigar, but Thursday proved him wrong. "This was just as good," the American said.

Unhappily the race claimed a fatality when Japanese challenger Hokuto Vega, a prolific winner in her own country, fell with about 400 metres to go. English-trained Bijou d'Inde was brought down but jockeys Norihiro Yokoyama and Jason Weaver escaped serious injury.
Meanwhile, the world is well and truly Singspiel's oyster.

The five-year-old has now won on three continents, appears to take travel in his stride and has proved himself equally at home on grass or dirt. After a suitable rest he is sure to be aimed once more at all the top middle-distance events.
